Ek verlede het somer na Rome gegaan.
af.f: Ek het verlede somer na Rome gegaan.
af.r: "Verlede somer" — last summer — sits neatly before the verb, and "na" marks the destination. "Het ... gegaan" bookends the sentence once more, as past tenses here are so terribly fond of doing.

travel.s: Where is the hotel located?

it.r: "Dove si trova", old chap — the reflexive construction, intact and in order. "Dove trova" alone simply trails off, as though the hotel found something instead.

fr.native_context: ‘Où se trouve’ is guidebook French. In real life people ask ‘Il est où, l’hôtel ?’
fr.roast_if_wrong: ‘Où se trouve’, how charmingly stiff. One is asking a passer-by, not addressing a parliament.
fr.r: "Où l'hôtel se trouve ?" has simply abandoned word order altogether, and "située" wrongly feminises itself — "hôtel" is masculine, so "situé" it must remain.

de.r: Inversion, my good man: "Wo befindet sich das Hotel?" — the verb comes second, always. A manual for the perfect incompetent clearly awaits you.

o: โรงแรมอยู่ที่ไหน
โรงแรมที่ไหนอยู่
ที่ไหนอยู่โรงแรม
โรงแรมอยู่ไหนที่
th.f: โรงแรมอยู่ที่ไหน
th.r: The question word “ที่ไหน” waits patiently at the very end, no inversion required — Thai doesn't share England's compulsion to march the verb to the front like a changing of the guard.

af.r: "Geleë" is a rather formal, literary past participle for "located" — and note the inversion for questions: the verb leaps ahead of its subject, "is die hotel", standing at attention the moment a question mark looms.

travel.s: We have stayed at the hotel for three days.

o: Soggiorniamo in hotel da tre giorni.
Soggiorniamo in hotel per tre giorni.
Abbiamo soggiornato in hotel da tre giorni.
Siamo stati in hotel da tre giorni.
it.f: Soggiorniamo in hotel da tre giorni.
it.r: "Da" with the present tense, my dear sir, exactly as with "depuis" and "seit" — a trio of languages agreeing on one rule you alone resist.

o: On est à l'hôtel depuis trois jours.
Cela fait trois jours que nous séjournons à l'hôtel.
Nous séjournons à l'hôtel pendant trois jours.
Nous avons séjourné à l'hôtel depuis trois jours.
fr.f: On est à l'hôtel depuis trois jours.
fr.natural_version: On est à l'hôtel depuis trois jours.
fr.literal_trap: Nous séjournons à l'hôtel depuis trois jours.
fr.native_context: ‘Séjourner’ is for brochures. In everyday speech people say ‘on est à…’, and ‘on’ replaces ‘nous’.
fr.roast_if_wrong: ‘Nous séjournons’? Quite the brochure, my dear. Real people say ‘on est à l’hôtel’.
fr.r: "Pendant" marks a bounded stretch of time, not an ongoing one — "depuis" is required here. And switching to the passé composé with "depuis" rather defeats the point: the stay isn't over yet.

o: Wir sind seit drei Tagen im Hotel.
Wir wohnen für drei Tage im Hotel.
Wir haben seit drei Tagen im Hotel gewohnt.
Wir sind seit drei Tagen im Hotel wohnen.
de.f: Wir sind seit drei Tagen im Hotel.
de.r: "Seit" with the present, my dear sir — the stay is still ongoing, so the tense must be too. Wake up to your own timeline before I lose patience.

o: เราพักที่โรงแรมมาสามวันแล้ว
เราพักที่โรงแรมมาวันสามแล้ว
เราพักที่โรงแรมแล้วมาสามวัน
เราที่โรงแรมพักมาวันสามแล้ว
th.f: เราพักที่โรงแรมมาสามวันแล้ว
th.r: “มา...แล้ว” wraps itself around the duration like a conga line at Songkran — don't scatter สามวัน outside the pair.

o: Ons bly al drie dae by die hotel.
Ons het al drie dae by die hotel bly.
Ons bly by die hotel al drie dag.
Ons al bly drie dae by die hotel.
af.f: Ons bly al drie dae by die hotel.
af.r: "Al drie dae" marks ongoing duration again, just as with the soup eaten "al twee uur" — and "by die hotel" uses "by", not "in", for staying at a place. Consistency, old chap, is Afrikaans's quiet virtue.

travel.s: Can you give me some advice?

it.r: "Qualche consiglio" stays singular after "qualche", my dear fellow, however many pieces of advice are implied. Italian's little inconsistency, and yours.

fr.r: "Quelques conseils", my dear fellow — plural, as advice rarely arrives singly. "Un conseils" manages to be both singular and plural at once, which is impressively wrong.

o: Kannst du mir ein paar Ratschläge geben?
Kannst du mir ein paar Ratschlag geben?
Kannst du mir etwas Ratschläge geben?
Kannst du mir ein paar Ratschlägen geben?
de.f: Kannst du mir ein paar Ratschläge geben?
de.r: "Ein paar Ratschläge" — the plural of "Ratschlag" is irregular, old sport, and you've avoided it entirely. Advice about you, I fear, simply doesn't take.

o: ช่วยให้คำแนะนำหน่อยได้ไหม
ช่วยให้แนะนำคำหน่อยได้ไหม
ช่วยคำแนะนำให้หน่อยได้ไหม
ให้ช่วยคำแนะนำหน่อยได้ไหม
th.f: ช่วยให้คำแนะนำหน่อยได้ไหม
th.r: “หน่อย” softens the request right before “ได้ไหม” seals it politely — drop the order and you'll sound less like a traveller, more like you're barking at a mae khaa over her som tam cart.

o: Kan jy vir my raad gee?
Kan jy vir my raad gee nie?
Kan vir jy my raad gee?
af.f: Kan jy vir my raad gee?
af.r: "Vir my" marks the recipient of the advice, and "raad gee" — give advice — is the fixed collocation. Do not go inventing your own; the Afrikaans ear is unforgiving on this point.

travel.s: I look forward to seeing Paris.

o: Non vedo l'ora di vedere Parigi.
Non vedo l'ora a vedere Parigi.
it.f: Non vedo l'ora di vedere Parigi.
it.r: "Di vedere" after "non vedo l'ora" — the preposition is fixed, my dear sir, and fixed phrases forgive nothing. Basic logic escapes you entirely.

fr.r: "Hâte de" plus the infinitive, my dear sir — "hâte à" simply isn't a construction French possesses. Basic prepositions escape you entirely.

o: Ich freue mich darauf, Paris zu sehen.
Ich freue mich auf, Paris zu sehen.
Ich freue mich darauf, Paris sehen.
Ich freue mich für, Paris zu sehen.
de.f: Ich freue mich darauf, Paris zu sehen.
de.r: "Sich freuen darauf... zu" — the "da-" compound is obligatory before an infinitive clause, old sport. Drop it and the sentence collapses mid-sentence.

o: ฉันรอไม่ไหวที่จะได้เห็นปารีส
ฉันรอไม่ไหวที่จะเห็นได้ปารีส
ฉันไม่รอไหวที่จะได้เห็นปารีส
ฉันรอไม่ที่จะไหวได้เห็นปารีส
th.f: ฉันรอไม่ไหวที่จะได้เห็นปารีส
th.r: “ที่จะ” bridges รอไม่ไหว to the thing you're longing for — skip it and your eagerness collapses into a grammatical fender-bender.

o: Ek sien uit daarna om Parys te sien.
Ek sien uit na om Parys te sien.
Ek sien uit daarna Parys te sien.
Ek uit sien daarna om Parys te sien.
af.f: Ek sien uit daarna om Parys te sien.
af.r: "Sien uit daarna om ... te sien" — look forward to seeing — is a separable verb, "uitsien", propped apart by "daarna" with the infinitive trailing after "om...te". A proper mouthful, I grant you, but satisfying once mastered.

travel.s: I lost my luggage at the airport.

o: Ho perso i miei bagagli in aeroporto.
Ho perso il mio bagagli in aeroporto.
Ho perso i bagagli ad aeroporto.
it.f: Ho perso i miei bagagli in aeroporto.
it.r: "I miei bagagli" — plural article, plural possessive, plural noun, all agreeing, my dear fellow. You've lost your luggage and your sense of agreement in one go.

o: J'ai perdu mes bagages à l'aéroport.
J'ai perdu mes bagage à l'aéroport.
J'ai perdu mon bagages à l'aéroport.
J'ai perdu les bagages à aéroport.
fr.f: J'ai perdu mes bagages à l'aéroport.
fr.r: "Mes bagages" — plural, my dear fellow, as luggage rarely travels as a single sad bag. "Mon bagages" mismatches singular and plural in one tragic word.

o: Ich habe mein Gepäck am Flughafen verloren.
Ich habe meine Gepäcke am Flughafen verloren.
Ich habe mein Gepäcks am Flughafen verloren.
Ich habe mein Gepäck an Flughafen verloren.
de.f: Ich habe mein Gepäck am Flughafen verloren.
de.r: "Mein Gepäck" — singular and uncountable in German, old sport, unlike in French or English. "Meine Gepäcke" invents a plural that simply does not exist.

o: ฉันทำกระเป๋าเดินทางหายที่สนามบิน
ฉันกระเป๋าเดินทางทำหายที่สนามบิน
ฉันทำกระเป๋าหายเดินทางที่สนามบิน
ที่สนามบินฉันหายทำกระเป๋าเดินทาง
th.f: ฉันทำกระเป๋าเดินทางหายที่สนามบิน
th.r: ทำ...หาย wraps around the lost object like a pickpocket's hand — กระเป๋าเดินทาง sits snugly inside, not loitering outside the construction.

o: Ek het my bagasie by die lughawe verloor.
Ek het my bagasie by die lughawe verloren.
Ek is my bagasie by die lughawe verloor.
Ek my het bagasie by die lughawe verloor.
af.f: Ek het my bagasie by die lughawe verloor.
af.r: "By die lughawe" — at the airport — uses "by" once again. Rather like misplacing one's luggage, this preposition shows up reliably in the same spot every time.

travel.s: We arrived in London late.

o: Siamo arrivati a Londra in ritardo.
it.f: Siamo arrivati a Londra in ritardo.
it.r: "In ritardo" is the set phrase, my dear chap — "tardo" describes a person's slowness of mind, which, under the circumstances, feels rather apt.

o: Nous sommes arrivés à Londres tardif.
Nous sommes arrivés à Londres en retard.
Nous avons arrivé à Londres tard.
Nous sommes arrivés au Londres tard.
fr.f: Nous sommes arrivés à Londres en retard.
fr.r: "En retard" is the fixed phrase for arriving late, my dear chap — "tardif" describes a season, not a traveller. No degree in French required, only a dictionary.

o: Wir sind spät in London angekommen.
Wir sind spät nach London angekommen.
Wir haben spät in London angekommen.
Wir sind spät zu London angekommen.
de.f: Wir sind spät in London angekommen.
de.r: "In London", old sport — the preposition of location, not motion, since you've already arrived. "Zu London" would mean you're still somehow en route.

o: เรามาถึงลอนดอนช้ากว่ากำหนด
เรามาถึงช้ากว่ากำหนดลอนดอน
เราถึงมาลอนดอนช้ากว่ากำหนด
เรามาถึงลอนดอนกำหนดช้ากว่า
th.f: เรามาถึงลอนดอนช้ากว่ากำหนด
th.r: ช้า trails at the very end, describing the whole arrival — shove it mid-sentence and London sounds less delayed, more like a crime scene.

o: Ons het laat in Londen aangekom.
Ons is laat in Londen aangekom.
Ons het in Londen laat aankom.
Ons laat het in Londen aangekom.
af.f: Ons het laat in Londen aangekom.
af.r: "Laat" — late — sits mid-sentence, and "aangekom" is the compound verb for "arrived", built from "aan" plus "kom". London, I'm afraid, remains unmoved by your tardiness regardless of word order.

travel.s: The flight was delayed due to rain.

o: Il volo è stato ritardato a causa della pioggia.
Il volo è stato ritardato a causa la pioggia.
Il volo è stato ritardato per causa della pioggia.
Il volo è stato ritardato a causa del pioggia.
it.f: Il volo è stato ritardato a causa della pioggia.
it.r: "A causa della pioggia" — "della" fuses "di" and "la", old sport. A causa la pioggia simply leaves the preposition stranded on the platform.

o: Le vol a été retardé à cause de la pluie.
Le vol a été retardé à cause la pluie.
Le vol a été retardé pour cause de la pluie.
Le vol a été retardé à cause du pluie.
fr.f: Le vol a été retardé à cause de la pluie.
fr.r: "À cause de la pluie" — "à cause de" plus the feminine article, old sport. Drop the "de" and you've blamed the rain for nothing at all.

o: Der Flug hatte wegen des Regens Verspätung.
Der Flug hat wegen des Regens verspätet.
Der Flug wegen des Regens hatte Verspätung.
Der Flug hatte wegen dem Regen Verspätung.
de.f: Der Flug hatte wegen des Regens Verspätung.
de.r: "Wegen des Regens" — "wegen" takes the genitive, my dear sir, hence "des Regens", not "dem Regen". Grammar regards you with compassion; I do not.

o: เที่ยวบินล่าช้าเพราะฝนตก
เที่ยวบินเพราะล่าช้าฝนตก
เพราะเที่ยวบินฝนตกล่าช้า
ล่าช้าเที่ยวบินเพราะฝนตก
th.f: เที่ยวบินล่าช้าเพราะฝนตก
th.r: ฝนตก is rain-falls, not falls-rain — swap the order and you've invented a new, rather violent weather event.

o: Die vlug is weens reën vertraag.
Die vlug is weens reën vertraagd.
Die vlug het weens reën vertraag is.
Die is vlug weens reën vertraag.
af.f: Die vlug is weens reën vertraag.
af.r: "Weens" means "due to, because of", and the whole clause sits in the passive: "is ... vertraag". The rain gets the blame; the flight simply suffers the consequences, grammatically speaking.

travel.s: I need to book a flight.

it.r: "Prenotare un volo", my dear chap — the verb takes its object directly, no "biglietto" grafted on where it doesn't belong. Be concise and precise.

o: Je dois réserver un billet d'avions.
Je dois réserver un vol billet.
Je dois réserver un billet de vol.
fr.r: "Réserver un vol", my dear chap — concise, as flight bookings should be. "Un vol billet" stacks two nouns like unclaimed baggage.

o: Ich muss ein Ticket des Flugs buchen.
de.r: "Einen Flug buchen" — accusative masculine, old sport, and no invented compound like "Flugtickets" required. Be precise, as the airline rarely is.

o: ฉันต้องจองเที่ยวบิน
ฉันจองต้องเที่ยวบิน
ฉันต้องเที่ยวบินจอง
ต้องฉันจองเที่ยวบิน
th.f: ฉันต้องจองเที่ยวบิน
th.r: ต้อง marches straight into the verb, no ‘to' required — rather like a monk on his morning almsround: no detours.

o: Ek moet om 'n vlug te bespreek.
af.r: "Bespreek" is "to book" or "reserve" here — though do remember the very same word reappears later meaning "discuss", a splendidly economical bit of Afrikaans polysemy.

travel.s: She missed the 5 PM train.

o: Ha perso il treno a le 17.
it.r: "Delle 17" — the hour takes its article and preposition fused, old sport. "Di 17" alone leaves the train without a proper time to miss.

o: Elle a raté le train de 17h.
Elle a raté le train de 17 heure.
Elle a raté le train à 17h de.
fr.f: Elle a raté le train de 17h.
fr.r: "Le train de 17h" — "de" links the train to its hour, old sport, not a stray preposition tacked onto the end. A golden rule you keep trampling.

o: Sie hat den Zug von 17 Uhr verpasst.
Sie hat den Zug um 17 Uhr verpasste.
Sie hat den 17 Uhr Zügen verpasst.
de.r: "Der 17-Uhr-Zug" — German loves a good compound noun, my dear sir, hyphens and all. Spell it out separately and you've missed the entire point of German.

o: เธอตกรถไฟตอนห้าโมงเย็น
เธอรถไฟตกตอนห้าโมงเย็น
เธอตกตอนรถไฟห้าโมงเย็น
เธอตกรถไฟตอนเย็นห้าโมง
th.f: เธอตกรถไฟตอนห้าโมงเย็น
th.r: ตกรถไฟ literally means ‘fell off the train' — poetic, if alarming — and ตอนห้าโมงเย็น trails at the end to say exactly when the tragedy struck.

af.r: "Vyfuur-trein" — the five-o'clock train — fuses into one hyphenated compound. Afrikaans loves gluing its nouns together rather than letting them drift apart like loose biltong strips.

travel.s: We visited the museum for three hours.

o: Abbiamo visitato il museo per tre ore.
Abbiamo visitato il museo durante tre ore.
Abbiamo visitato il museo in tre ore.
Abbiamo visitato il museo da tre ore.
it.f: Abbiamo visitato il museo per tre ore.
it.r: "Per tre ore" — "per" for a bounded duration, my dear fellow, not "durante", which implies something else entirely happening throughout. Precision, please.

o: Nous avons visité le musée pendant trois heures.
Nous avons visité le musée pour trois heures.
Nous avons visité le musée durante trois heures.
Nous avons visité le musée en trois heures.
fr.f: Nous avons visité le musée pendant trois heures.
fr.r: "Pendant", my dear fellow — a bounded, finished stretch of time, exactly what three hours at a museum once was. An error that makes dictionaries genuinely weep.

o: Wir waren drei Stunden lang im Museum.
Wir haben das Museum für drei Stunde besucht.
Wir haben das Museum währenden drei Stunden besucht.
Wir haben das Museum in drei Stunden besucht.
de.f: Wir waren drei Stunden lang im Museum.
de.r: "Drei Stunden lang" — "lang" follows the duration in German, old sport, rather than a preposition up front. Three hours of art, apparently none of grammar.

o: เราเที่ยวชมพิพิธภัณฑ์สามชั่วโมง
เราเที่ยวชมพิพิธภัณฑ์ชั่วโมงสาม
เราเที่ยวสามชั่วโมงชมพิพิธภัณฑ์
เราเที่ยวชมสามพิพิธภัณฑ์ชั่วโมง
th.f: เราเที่ยวชมพิพิธภัณฑ์สามชั่วโมง
th.r: The duration สามชั่วโมง follows the verb directly, no preposition required — Thai doesn't bother with England's beloved ‘for'; it simply gets on with the museum.

o: Ons het die museum drie uur lank besoek.
Ons is die museum drie uur lank besoek.
Ons het die museum drie uur lank besoeken.
Ons die het museum drie uur lank besoek.
af.f: Ons het die museum drie uur lank besoek.
af.r: "Drie uur lank" tacks "lank" — long — onto the duration, the equivalent of English's "for three hours". Museums, it seems, demand their due in both languages.

travel.s: The passport control officer asked for ID.

o: L'addetto al controllo passaporti ha chiesto un documenti.
L'addetto al controllo passaporti chiede un documento.
L'addetto al controllo passaporti ha chiesto un documento d'identità.
L'addetto al controllo passaporti ha chiedere un documento.
it.f: L'addetto al controllo passaporti ha chiesto un documento d'identità.
it.r: "Ha chiesto" — past tense, my dear sir, the irregular participle of "chiedere". Were you watching the clouds, or merely watching the wrong verb?

o: L'agent au contrôle des passeports a demandé une pièce d'identité.
L'agent du contrôle des passeports demande une pièce d'identité.
L'agent du contrôle des passeports a demandé une pièce identité.
L'agent du contrôle des passeports a demander une pièce d'identité.
fr.f: L'agent au contrôle des passeports a demandé une pièce d'identité.
fr.r: "A demandé" — the passé composé, my dear sir, not the present tense wandering in from another sentence. Were you watching the clouds during this exchange?

o: Der Grenzbeamte hat einen Ausweis verlangt.
Der Passkontrolleur hat einen Ausweis verlangen.
Der Passkontrolleur hat einen Ausweis verlangt gehabt.
de.f: Der Grenzbeamte hat einen Ausweis verlangt.
de.r: "Hat verlangt" — past tense needed, old sport, since the officer already asked and you've presumably already handed over your passport by now.

o: เจ้าหน้าที่ตรวจหนังสือเดินทางขอดูบัตรประจำตัว
เจ้าหน้าที่ตรวจหนังสือเดินทางดูขอบัตรประจำตัว
เจ้าหน้าที่ขอตรวจหนังสือเดินทางประจำบัตรตัว
ขอเจ้าหน้าที่ตรวจหนังสือเดินทางดูบัตรประจำตัว
th.f: เจ้าหน้าที่ตรวจหนังสือเดินทางขอดูบัตรประจำตัว
th.r: เจ้าหน้าที่ตรวจหนังสือเดินทาง is one long compound noun, glued together like sticky rice — prise it apart and the officer dissolves into confused fragments.

o: Die paspoortbeampte het vir identifikasie gevra.
Die paspoortbeampte het vir identifikasie gevragt.
Die paspoortbeampte is vir identifikasie gevra.
Die het paspoortbeampte vir identifikasie gevra.
af.f: Die paspoortbeampte het vir identifikasie gevra.
af.r: "Vir identifikasie" marks what was asked for, with "vir" doing the work English hands to "for". And "paspoortbeampte" is another of those satisfying compound nouns, officer of the passport, all in one breath.

travel.s: I left my keys at home yesterday.

o: Ho lasciata le chiavi a casa ieri.
Ho lasciato le chiavi a casa ieri.
Dimentico le chiavi a casa ieri.
Ho lasciato le chiavi casa a ieri.
it.f: Ho lasciato le chiavi a casa ieri.
it.r: "Lasciato" — masculine past participle, my dear chap, agreeing with nothing feminine in sight. "Lasciata" would suggest the keys themselves did the leaving.

o: J'ai oublier mes clés à la maison hier.
J'ai laissé mes clés à la maison hier.
J'oublie mes clés à la maison hier.
J'ai oublié mes clés dans maison hier.
fr.f: J'ai laissé mes clés à la maison hier.
fr.r: "Laissé", my dear chap — the past participle of "laisser", to leave behind. "Oublier" conjugated wrong manages to compound one error atop another.

o: Ich habe gestern die Schlüssel zu Hause vergessene.
Ich habe gestern die Schlüssel zu Hause gelassen.
Ich vergesse gestern die Schlüssel zu Hause.
Ich habe gestern die Schlüssel in Haus vergessen.
de.f: Ich habe gestern die Schlüssel zu Hause gelassen.
de.r: "Gelassen" — the correct participle of "lassen", old sport, not an invented form of "vergessen" mangled beyond recognition. Basic notions, badly misplaced.

o: เมื่อวานฉันลืมกุญแจไว้ที่บ้าน
เมื่อวานฉันลืมไว้กุญแจที่บ้าน
เมื่อวานฉันลืมกุญแจที่บ้านไว้
เมื่อวานฉันกุญแจลืมที่ไว้บ้าน
th.f: เมื่อวานฉันลืมกุญแจไว้ที่บ้าน
th.r: ลืม...ไว้ที่ wraps around where you abandoned your keys — rather like leaving your dignity at a night market stall and never going back for it.

o: Ek het gister my sleutels by die huis vergeet.
Ek het gister my sleutels by die huis vergeten.
Ek is gister my sleutels by die huis vergeet.
Ek gister het my sleutels by die huis vergeet.
af.f: Ek het gister my sleutels by die huis vergeet.
af.r: "Gister" — yesterday — slots neatly mid-sentence, and "by die huis" is, once again, "at home". The keys, alas, remain exactly where left, irrespective of your command of Afrikaans word order.

travel.s: How long does it take?

it.r: "Quanto tempo ci vuole?" — "ci vuole" is the fixed idiom for how long something takes, my dear sir. Thank heavens you travel; your idioms rather less so.

fr.native_context: ‘Combien de temps faut-il ?’ is correct but formal; people say ‘Ça prend combien de temps ?’
fr.roast_if_wrong: ‘Faut-il’? Do mind the 1960s calling, my dear fellow. ‘Ça prend combien de temps ?’
fr.r: "Combien du temps" smuggles in a partitive that has no business being there, and "combien temps" simply forgets its "de" altogether — a rather careless way to ask how long something takes.

de.r: "Wie lange", old sport — the standard phrase for duration. "Wie viel Zeit" isn't wrong exactly, merely the long way round a short question.

o: ใช้เวลานานแค่ไหน
ใช้นานเวลาแค่ไหน
ใช้เวลาแค่ไหนนาน
นานเวลาใช้แค่ไหน
th.f: ใช้เวลานานแค่ไหน
th.r: แค่ไหน closes the question, every time — put it up front and you'll sound like you're accusing the duration itself of a crime.

af.r: "Hoe lank" — how long — triggers the familiar inversion, verb leaping to meet its question word like a dog to a Sunday braai.

travel.s: We rented a car to get around.

o: Abbiamo noleggiato un'auto per spostarci in città.
Abbiamo noleggiato un'auto per muoverci a città.
Abbiamo noleggiato un'auto per girando in città.
Abbiamo noleggiato un'auto a spostarci in città.
it.f: Abbiamo noleggiato un'auto per spostarci in città.
it.r: "Per spostarci", my dear chap — "per" plus infinitive for purpose, the reflexive attached neatly to the end. Tune into the real language, not the broken one.

o: Nous avons loué une voiture pour nous déplacer en ville.
Nous avons loué une voiture pour bouger en ville.
Nous avons loué une voiture pour circulant en ville.
Nous avons loué une voiture à nous déplacer en ville.
fr.f: Nous avons loué une voiture pour nous déplacer en ville.
fr.r: "Pour nous déplacer", my dear chap — "pour" plus infinitive expresses purpose. "À nous déplacer" simply isn't how French expresses getting around.

o: Wir haben ein Auto gemietet, um in der Stadt herumzufahren.
Wir haben ein Auto gemietet, um uns in der Stadt zu bewegt.
Wir haben ein Auto gemietet, für uns in der Stadt fortzubewegen.
Wir haben ein Auto gemietet, um in der Stadt fortbewegen.
de.f: Wir haben ein Auto gemietet, um in der Stadt herumzufahren.
de.r: "Um uns ... fortzubewegen" — the "um...zu" construction wraps around the whole clause, old sport, reflexive pronoun included. Tune into the real language.

o: เราเช่ารถเพื่อเดินทางไปรอบเมือง
เราเช่ารถเพื่อเดินทางรอบไปเมือง
เราเช่าเพื่อรถเดินทางไปรอบเมือง
เราเพื่อเช่ารถเดินทางไปรอบเมือง
th.f: เราเช่ารถเพื่อเดินทางไปรอบเมือง
th.r: เพื่อ introduces purpose, and the verbs queue up after it in order — a proper queue, mind, unlike the scrum for a tuk-tuk outside Chatuchak.

o: Ons het 'n motor gehuur om rond te kom.
Ons het 'n motor gehuurd om rond te kom.
Ons het 'n motor gehuur om rond kom.
Ons 'n het motor gehuur om rond te kom.
af.f: Ons het 'n motor gehuur om rond te kom.
af.r: "Om rond te kom" — to get around — uses the separable "rondkom" with the "om...te" infinitive bridging the gap. Hiring the car was the easy part, old chap.

travel.s: The map was unreadable.

it.r: "Illeggibile" — one word, properly formed, my dear sir. "Nonleggibile" glues two pieces together that Italian has never agreed to share a sentence.

fr.r: "Illisible", my dear sir — one prefix, one adjective. "Inlisible" invents a prefix French has never once used; your mental map is quite beyond recovery.

de.r: "Unleserlich" — the correct negative prefix, old sport, not some wandering "-en" ending bolted on for no reason. Quite beyond recovery, like your sense of direction.

o: แผนที่อ่านไม่ออก
แผนที่อ่านออกไม่
แผนที่ไม่ออกอ่าน
อ่านไม่แผนที่ออก
th.f: แผนที่อ่านไม่ออก
th.r: อ่านไม่ออก is the ‘can't manage to' construction — the map isn't simply unreadable, it has personally defeated you, which is rather more dramatic and rather more accurate.

af.r: "Onleesbaar" fuses the negative prefix "on-" straight onto "leesbaar" (readable) — one tidy compound adjective where English needs two separate words to make the same complaint.

travel.s: I need accommodation.

it.r: "Un alloggio", my dear sir — the correct noun entirely, not "alloggia" nor "alloggi", both of which are simply other words wearing a disguise. What a disaster.

fr.r: "Un logement", my dear sir — masculine, singular, unremarkable. "Du logement" turns a simple need into a partitive disaster.

de.r: "Eine Unterkunft", old sport — feminine, as German nouns so often surprise you by being. "Einen Unterkunft" mismatches gender and case in one breath.

o: ฉันต้องการที่พัก
ฉันที่พักต้องการ
ฉันต้องการพักที่
ต้องการฉันที่พัก
th.f: ฉันต้องการที่พัก
th.r: ต้องการ takes its noun plain, no extra fuss — Thai needs no dressing-up to ask for accommodation, unlike you, clutching a phrasebook at check-in.

af.r: "Het ... nodig" returns for accommodation, exactly as it did for the under-salted soup. Afrikaans, you'll find, is admirably consistent about what it deems "necessary".

travel.s: We crossed the border without any problems.

o: Abbiamo attraversato il confine senza problemi.
Abbiamo attraversato il confine senza problemo.
Abbiamo attraversato il confine senza dei problemi.
Abbiamo attraversato il confine senza alcun problemi.
it.f: Abbiamo attraversato il confine senza problemi.
it.r: "Senza problemi", my dear chap — plural, as across three languages now. A rare joy that doesn't erase your slips, merely postpones noticing them.

o: Nous avons traversé la frontière sans problèmes.
Nous avons traversé la frontière sans problèmo.
Nous avons traversé la frontière sans des problèmes.
Nous avons traversé la frontière sans aucun problèmes.
fr.f: Nous avons traversé la frontière sans problèmes.
fr.r: "Sans problèmes", my dear chap — plural after "sans" here, as problems so rarely arrive alone. A rare joy that doesn't erase your other slips.

o: Wir haben die Grenze ohne Probleme überquert.
Wir haben die Grenze ohne Problem überquert.
Wir haben die Grenze ohne Probleme überqueren.
Wir haben die Grenze ohne Probleme überquert gehabt.
de.f: Wir haben die Grenze ohne Probleme überquert.
de.r: "Ohne Probleme" — plural, old sport, matching the French rather nicely for once. Borders crossed without incident; your grammar, less fortunate.

o: เราข้ามชายแดนได้โดยไม่มีปัญหาเลย
เราข้ามชายแดนได้โดยมีไม่ปัญหาเลย
เราข้ามได้ชายแดนโดยไม่มีปัญหาเลย
เราข้ามชายแดนโดยได้ไม่มีปัญหาเลย
th.f: เราข้ามชายแดนได้โดยไม่มีปัญหาเลย
th.r: โดยไม่มีปัญหาเลย closes the sentence with เลย for emphasis — leave it off and you've crossed the border with merely ‘no problem', a much weaker claim than ‘none whatsoever.'

o: Ons het die grens sonder enige probleme oorgesteek.
Ons het die grens sonder enige probleme oorgesteken.
Ons het die grens oorgesteek sonder enige probleme nie.
Ons die het grens sonder enige probleme oorgesteek.
af.f: Ons het die grens sonder enige probleme oorgesteek.
af.r: "Sonder enige probleme" — without any problems — and "oorgesteek", the compound verb for "crossed" built from "oor" (over) plus "steek" (pierce/cross). The border, like the sentence, gets traversed cleanly.

travel.s: The tourist guide spoke very well.

o: La guida turistica ha parlato molto bene.
La guida turistica ha parlato molto buono.
La guida turistica ha parlato molto bene bene.
La guida turistica ha parla molto bene.
it.f: La guida turistica ha parlato molto bene.
it.r: "Molto bene" is the adverb, my dear sir — "molto buono" would mean the guide himself was tasty. An understandable confusion, if a culinary one.

o: Le guide touristique a très bien parlé.
Le guide touristique a très bon parlé.
Le guide touristique a parlé très bon.
Le guide touristique a parlé très bon bien.
fr.f: Le guide touristique a très bien parlé.
fr.r: "Très bien" is the adverb, my dear sir — "très bon" describes a noun, and your guide, however gifted, is not himself delicious.

o: Der Tourguide hat sehr gut gesprochen.
Der Reiseführer hat sehr gute gesprochen.
Der Reiseführer hat sehr gut gesprochen gehabt.
de.f: Der Tourguide hat sehr gut gesprochen.
de.r: "Sehr gut" — the adverb stays uninflected, old sport. "Sehr gute" adds an ending that belongs only to adjectives modifying nouns. Elementary.

o: ไกด์นำเที่ยวพูดเก่งมาก
ไกด์นำเที่ยวมากพูดเก่ง
ไกด์เที่ยวนำพูดเก่งมาก
นำเที่ยวไกด์พูดเก่งมาก
th.f: ไกด์นำเที่ยวพูดเก่งมาก
th.r: พูดเก่ง glues the skill directly onto the verb, no separate adverb needed — the guide simply ‘speaks skilled,' which saves everyone the bother England insists upon.

o: Die toergids het baie goed gepraat.
Die toergids het baie goed gepraten.
Die toergids het gepraat baie goed.
Die het toergids baie goed gepraat.
af.f: Die toergids het baie goed gepraat.
af.r: "Baie goed" — very well — sits before the verb it modifies has finished its business, a touch different from English's habit of tucking such adverbs at the end.

travel.s: I am travelling on my own.

o: Sto viaggiando da solo per mio conto.
Sto viaggiando da solo con il mio.
it.r: "Da solo" is the fixed expression, my dear sir — repeating "solo" twice merely emphasises how alone you've left your grammar.

fr.r: "Seul" is the set word for travelling alone, my dear sir — "par mon propre" is an invention with no home in French. Learn the set phrases.

de.r: "Allein" — one tidy adverb, old sport, not a wandering prepositional phrase about one's own company. Learn the set phrases; they exist for a reason.

o: ฉันเดินทางคนเดียว
ฉันเดินทางเดียวคน
ฉันเดินทางหนึ่งคนเดียว
เดินทางฉันคนเดียว
th.f: ฉันเดินทางคนเดียว
th.r: คนเดียว trails the verb as one unit, literally ‘one person' — split it up and you'll sound as though you've multiplied mid-journey, which even mai pen rai can't excuse.

af.r: "Alleen" — alone — trails to the very end, and note the plain present tense doing double duty for an ongoing action. Afrikaans has little patience for English's fussy "-ing" continuous forms.

sports.s: Our team played very well yesterday.

o: La nostra squadra ha giocato molto bene ieri.
La nostra squadra ha giocato molto buono ieri.
La nostra squadra ha gioca molto bene ieri.
La nostra squadra ha giocato bene molto ieri.
it.f: La nostra squadra ha giocato molto bene ieri.
it.r: "Molto bene" — the adverb, my dear fellow, not "molto buono", which would mean your team was somehow delicious rather than merely victorious.

o: Notre équipe a très bien joué hier.
Notre équipe a très bon joué hier.
Notre équipe a joué très bon hier.
Notre équipe a joué très biens hier.
fr.f: Notre équipe a très bien joué hier.
fr.r: "Très bien" is the adverb, my dear fellow — "très biens" invents a plural for a word that never takes one. Not even in the schoolyard would that pass.

o: Unsere Mannschaft hat gestern sehr gut gespielt.
Unsere Mannschaft hat gestern sehr gute gespielt.
Unsere Mannschaft hat gestern sehr gut gespielt gehabt.
Unsere Mannschaft spielte gestern sehr gute.
de.f: Unsere Mannschaft hat gestern sehr gut gespielt.
de.r: "Sehr gut" — uninflected, old sport, however badly you want to dress it up. "Sehr gute" borrows an ending meant for adjectives, not adverbs.

o: เมื่อวานทีมของเราเล่นได้ดีมาก
เมื่อวานทีมเราของเล่นได้ดีมาก
เมื่อวานทีมของเราเล่นดีได้มาก
ทีมของเราเมื่อวานเล่นมากได้ดี
th.f: เมื่อวานทีมของเราเล่นได้ดีมาก
th.r: เมื่อวาน opens the sentence like a true topic, not tucked in at the back English-style — and “เล่นได้ดี” is the resultative ‘play-and-succeed-well' construction, not a bolted-on adverb.

o: Ons span het gister baie goed gespeel.
Ons span het gister baie goed gespeelt.
Ons span het gister gespeel baie goed.
Ons het span gister baie goed gespeel.
af.f: Ons span het gister baie goed gespeel.
af.r: "Gister" and "baie goed" both queue up before the past participle "gespeel" — Afrikaans likes its adverbs fashionably early, rather unlike English's tendency to let them trail the field.

sports.s: He ran faster than everyone else.

o: Ha corso più veloce di chiunque altro.
Ha corso più veloce che chiunque altro.
Ha corso più veloce di chiunque altri.
Ha corse più veloce di chiunque altro.
it.f: Ha corso più veloce di chiunque altro.
it.r: "Più veloce di chiunque altro" — "di" for comparisons, my dear sir, not "che". Even the goalposts know it, and goalposts have notoriously little education.

o: Il a couru plus vite que tout le monde.
Il a couru plus rapide que quiconque.
Il a couru plus vite de quiconque.
Il courait plus vite que quiconque.
fr.f: Il a couru plus vite que tout le monde.
fr.r: "Plus vite que", my dear sir — comparison takes "que", never "de". Even the goalposts know that much, and they don't speak French at all.

o: Er ist schneller gelaufen als alle anderen.
Er hat schneller gelaufen als alle anderen.
Er ist schneller gelaufen wie alle anderen.
Er ist schneller laufen als alle anderen.
de.f: Er ist schneller gelaufen als alle anderen.
de.r: "Als alle anderen" — "als" for comparisons in German, old sport, not "wie", which is reserved for similarity. He ran faster; you compared worse.

o: เขาวิ่งเร็วกว่าคนอื่นทุกคน
เขาวิ่งกว่าเร็วคนอื่นทุกคน
เขาเร็วกว่าวิ่งคนอื่นทุกคน
เขาวิ่งเร็วคนอื่นกว่าทุกคน
th.f: เขาวิ่งเร็วกว่าคนอื่นทุกคน
th.r: เร็วกว่า keeps the comparative glued right after the adjective — wander “กว่า” off on its own and you've run faster than grammar itself.

o: Hy het vinniger as enigiemand anders gehardloop.
Hy het vinniger dan enigiemand anders gehardloop.
Hy het meer vinnig as enigiemand anders gehardloop.
Hy het vinniger as enigiemand ander gehardloop.
af.f: Hy het vinniger as enigiemand anders gehardloop.
af.r: "Vinniger as" is your comparative — faster than — and "enigiemand anders" covers "anyone else" tidily in two words. He outran the lot of them, grammatically speaking and otherwise.

sports.s: She doesn't like playing tennis.

o: Non le piace giocare a tennis.
Non le piace giocare in tennis.
Non le piace giocare a il tennis.
it.f: Non le piace giocare a tennis.
it.r: "A tennis" — the fixed preposition for sports played, old sport, unlike "al tennis" or none at all. A pillar has collapsed upon you, and it wasn't the net.

o: Elle n'aime pas jouer au tennis.
Elle ne aime pas jouer au tennis.
Elle n'aime pas joué au tennis.
Elle n'aime pas jouer à le tennis.
fr.f: Elle n'aime pas jouer au tennis.
fr.r: "N'aime pas" — the negation wraps "n'" around the verb, old sport, never "ne" standing alone before a vowel. A pillar of French has collapsed upon you.

o: Sie spielt nicht gerne Tennis spielen.
Sie spielt nicht gern Tennis zu spielen.
Sie mag nicht Tennis spielen gern.
de.r: "Nicht gern" is the fixed way to dislike an activity in German, my dear fellow — "nicht gerne... spielen zu" doubles up on machinery that was never needed.

o: เธอไม่ชอบเล่นเทนนิส
เธอไม่เล่นชอบเทนนิส
ไม่เธอชอบเล่นเทนนิส
เธอชอบเล่นไม่เทนนิส
th.f: เธอไม่ชอบเล่นเทนนิส
th.r: ไม่ sits directly before ชอบ, no detours — and เล่นเทนนิส needs no ‘to play', Thai verbs happily queue up back to back, rather like stalls at a night market.

o: Sy hou nie daarvan om tennis te speel nie.
Sy hou nie daarvan om tennis te speel.
Sy hou nie daarvan tennis te speel om nie.
Sy nie hou daarvan om tennis te speel nie.
af.f: Sy hou nie daarvan om tennis te speel nie.
af.r: That "nie...nie" bracket is back in force, wrapping the whole "doesn't like playing tennis" — and "hou van" (like) splits apart as "hou...daarvan" with the infinitive dangling after "om...te". A proper grammatical obstacle course, old chap.

sports.s: My teammate and I won.

o: Il mio compagno di squadra e io abbiamo vinto.
Io e il mio compagno di squadra ha vinto.
Me e il mio compagno di squadra abbiamo vinto.
Il mio compagno di squadra e me abbiamo vinto.
it.f: Il mio compagno di squadra e io abbiamo vinto.
it.r: "Il mio compagno e io" — "io", not "me", stands as subject in Italian, my dear sir, however casual the sentence feels. A matter of manners, as ever.

o: Mon coéquipier et moi avons gagné.
Moi et mon coéquipier avons gagné.
Mon coéquipier et moi avons gagnés.
Mon coéquipier et je avons gagné.
fr.f: Mon coéquipier et moi avons gagné.
fr.r: "Mon coéquipier et moi" — the stressed pronoun "moi" comes last, my dear sir, a matter of manners as old as French itself. Mind your elders, grammatically speaking.

o: Mein Teamkollege und ich haben gewonnen.
Ich und mein Teamkollege haben gewonnen.
Mich und mein Teamkollege haben gewonnen.
Mein Teamkollege und mich haben gewonnen.
de.f: Mein Teamkollege und ich haben gewonnen.
de.r: "Mein Teamkollege und ich" — nominative "ich", old sport, never the accusative "mich" wandering in uninvited. A matter of manners, and of case.

o: ฉันกับเพื่อนร่วมทีมชนะ
ฉันกับชนะเพื่อนร่วมทีม
ฉันเพื่อนร่วมทีมกับชนะ
ฉันชนะกับเพื่อนร่วมทีมกับ
th.f: ฉันกับเพื่อนร่วมทีมชนะ
th.r: ฉันกับเพื่อนร่วมทีม bundles neatly together as the subject before ชนะ — no English-style etiquette demanding you name your teammate first, Thai just lines everyone up and wins.

o: My spanmaat en ek het gewen.
My spanmaat en my het gewen.
My spanmaat en ek is gewen.
My en spanmaat ek het gewen.
af.f: My spanmaat en ek het gewen.
af.r: "My spanmaat en ek" lines up teammate before self, same polite order English favours — Afrikaans simply confirms what you already suspected about manners. "Het gewen" closes things out, the victory bookended as every past tense here insists on being.

sports.s: The referee has made a mistake.

it.r: "Ha fatto" — the irregular participle of "fare", my dear sir, not a regularised invention. The only one deserving a card here is your grammar.

fr.r: "A fait" — "faire", not "faisait" nor an invented plural auxiliary. The only one deserving a red card here, I'm afraid, is your verb conjugation.

o: Der Schiedsrichter hat einen Fehler gemacht.
Der Schiedsrichter haben einen Fehler gemacht.
Der Schiedsrichter hat einen Fehler machen.
Der Schiedsrichter hat ein Fehler gemacht.
de.f: Der Schiedsrichter hat einen Fehler gemacht.
de.r: "Hat gemacht" — singular auxiliary for a singular referee, old sport, however many mistakes he made. The only one deserving a red card is you.

o: กรรมการทำผิดพลาด
กรรมการผิดพลาดทำ
ทำกรรมการผิดพลาด
กรรมการผิดทำพลาด
th.f: กรรมการทำผิดพลาด
th.r: ทำผิดพลาด is one tight compound, no ‘has' required to prop it up — Thai verbs don't need English's bureaucracy of auxiliaries.

af.r: "Fout maak" — make a mistake — is the fixed collocation the referee has, regrettably, fulfilled to the letter.

sports.s: He scored three goals.

it.r: "Tre gol" — invariable in the plural, old sport, resisting any Italian urge to add an ending. You, alas, score rather more own goals than he does.

fr.r: "Trois buts" — plural with an "s", old sport, as goals, mercifully for him, come in multiples. You, alas, tend to score rather more own goals.

de.r: "Drei Tore" — the correct plural, my dear fellow, not "Toren", which happens to mean fools. An unfortunate substitution, if an apt one.

o: เขายิงได้สามประตู
เขายิงได้ประตูสาม
เขาสามยิงได้ประตู
เขายิงสามได้ประตู
th.f: เขายิงได้สามประตู
th.r: ยิงได้ is the ‘shoot-and-succeed' pair — don't separate them — and สามประตู keeps the classifier ประตู snug against the number, same rule as sticky rice portions at a stall.

af.r: "Doele aangeteken" uses "aanteken" — register, log, score — and note "doele" takes the plural "-e" ending. Three goals, properly tallied, like runs on a scoreboard.

sports.s: We won against Milan.

o: Abbiamo vinto in opposizione al Milan.
it.r: "Contro il Milan" — the article stays with the club's name, my dear fellow, even when "contro" precedes it. What confusion, over something this routine.

o: Nous avons gagné contre à Milan.
Nous avons gagné en opposition à Milan.
fr.r: "Contre Milan", my dear fellow — "contre" alone suffices against a team. "En opposition à" turns a football match into a parliamentary debate.

o: Wir haben gegen Milan gewonnen gehabt.
Wir haben gegen zu Milan gewonnen.
de.r: "Gegen Milan" — accusative preposition, old sport, no dative tangled in beside it. What confusion, to lose a match of prepositions this simple.

o: เราชนะทีมมิลาน
เราชนะต่อต้านมิลาน
เราชนะมิลานทีม
ชนะเราทีมมิลาน
th.f: เราชนะทีมมิลาน
th.r: ชนะ takes its opponent straight on, no ‘against' required — Thai verbs don't flinch, they just win.

af.r: "Teen" marks the opponent — against — paired simply with "wen" (win). No fuss, no extra scaffolding; Milan simply loses, grammatically unadorned.

sports.s: The match ended in a draw.

o: La partita è finita in pareggio.
La partita è finita con pareggio.
La partita è finita per pareggio.
La partita è finita a pareggio.
it.f: La partita è finita in pareggio.
it.r: "In pareggio", my dear sir — the fixed phrase for a draw. "Con pareggio" or "per pareggio" are impostors wearing the right preposition for the wrong job.

o: Le match s'est terminé par un match nul.
Le match a terminé par un match nul.
Le match s'est terminé sur un nuls.
Le match s'est fini en nuls.
fr.f: Le match s'est terminé par un match nul.
fr.r: "S'est terminé par" — the reflexive, naturally, my dear sir, no needless passive construction required. The match ended plainly; let the sentence do the same.

o: Das Spiel endete mit einem Unentschieden.
Das Spiel wurde mit einem Unentschieden beendet.
Das Spiel hat mit einem Unentschieden geendeten.
Das Spiel endete zu einem Unentschieden.
de.f: Das Spiel endete mit einem Unentschieden.
de.r: "Endete mit" — the simple past, active, old sport, no passive frills needed for a result this ordinary. Keep your grammar as unadorned as the scoreline.

o: การแข่งขันจบลงด้วยการเสมอกัน
การแข่งขันจบด้วยลงการเสมอกัน
การแข่งขันลงจบด้วยการเสมอกัน
การแข่งขันจบลงเสมอด้วยกันการ
th.f: การแข่งขันจบลงด้วยการเสมอกัน
th.r: จบลงด้วย needs its nominalized partner การเสมอกัน — Thai turns the draw itself into a noun, a tidy little parcel, rather than describing it as an action.

o: Die wedstryd het in 'n gelykopuitslag geëindig.
Die wedstryd het in 'n gelykopuitslag geëindigd.
Die wedstryd het geëindig in gelykopuitslag 'n.
Die het wedstryd in 'n gelykopuitslag geëindig.
af.f: Die wedstryd het in 'n gelykopuitslag geëindig.
af.r: "Gelykopuitslag" is a splendid compound noun for "draw" — equal-up-result, all welded into one word. And "geëindig" wears its little diaeresis mark (ë) to keep the vowels from running into each other after that "ge-" prefix.

sports.s: She practices yoga every morning.

o: Lei pratica lo yoga ogni mattina.
it.f: Lei pratica lo yoga ogni mattina.
it.r: "Lo yoga" — masculine article before a word borrowed wholesale from elsewhere, my dear sir. An immense stroke of luck you got the article right at all.

o: Elle fait du yoga chaque matin.
Elle pratique le yoga tous les matin.
Elle pratiques le yoga chaque matin.
fr.f: Elle fait du yoga chaque matin.
fr.r: "Le yoga" with its article, my dear sir — French rarely lets a noun go bare. An immense stroke of luck that the rest of the sentence held together at all.

de.r: "Praktiziert" — third person singular, old sport, with its "-t" ending firmly attached. An immense stroke of luck, yoga aside, that you remembered the verb at all.

o: เธอเล่นโยคะทุกเช้า
เธอเล่นโยคะเช้าทุก
เธอทุกเล่นโยคะเช้า
เธอเล่นทุกเช้าโยคะ
th.f: เธอเล่นโยคะทุกเช้า
th.r: เล่นโยคะ borrows the verb for ‘play', even for yoga — don't reach for a stiffer word, Thai keeps its spiritual stretching refreshingly casual.

af.r: "Elke oggend" — every morning — sits before the verb's object, and note she "doen" yoga rather than "speel" it, unlike tennis earlier. Afrikaans, like a proper instructor, insists on the correct verb for the correct discipline.

sports.s: He threw the ball to me.

o: Mi ha lanciato la palla a mi.
it.r: "Mi ha lanciato" — the participle stays masculine, old sport, agreeing with "palla" not required here with "avere". Do stop inventing conjugations of your own.

o: Il m'a lancé la balle à moi.
fr.r: "M'a lancé" — the reflexive object pronoun does the work alone, old sport; "à moi" tacked on afterward simply repeats yourself twice.

o: Er hat mir den Ball zugeworfen.
Er hat mir den Ball geworfen zu.
Er hat mich den Ball zugeworfen.
Er hat mir der Ball zugeworfen.
de.f: Er hat mir den Ball zugeworfen.
de.r: "Mir den Ball" — dative for the receiver, accusative for the ball, my dear sir, each case exactly where it belongs. Do stop inventing conjugations.

o: เขาโยนลูกบอลมาให้ฉัน
เขาโยนมาลูกบอลให้ฉัน
เขาโยนลูกบอลให้มาฉัน
เขาลูกบอลโยนมาให้ฉัน
th.f: เขาโยนลูกบอลมาให้ฉัน
th.r: โยน...มาให้ strings three verbs in a row — throw, come, give — each pointing the ball exactly toward you. Drop “มา” and the ball's direction becomes anyone's guess.

o: Hy het die bal vir my gegooi.
Hy het die bal vir my gegooit.
Hy het gegooi die bal vir my.
Hy die het bal vir my gegooi.
af.f: Hy het die bal vir my gegooi.
af.r: "Vir my" marks the recipient once more, and "gegooi" is the past participle of "throw" — ge- plus the stem, bookended as ever by "het".

sports.s: The stadium was full of fans.

o: Lo stadio era pieno di tifosi.
Lo stadio era pieno con tifosi.
Lo stadio era pieno da tifosi.
Lo stadio era pieno dei tifosi.
it.f: Lo stadio era pieno di tifosi.
it.r: "Pieno di tifosi" — "di", my dear fellow, not "con" nor "da", both imposters in a sentence about a packed stadium. Shall I repeat it?

o: Le stade était plein de supporters.
Le stade était plein avec des supporters.
Le stade était plein par des supporters.
Le stade était rempli des supporters.
fr.f: Le stade était plein de supporters.
fr.r: "Plein de", my dear fellow — the fixed phrase for a packed stadium. "Rempli des" exists, certainly, but not in the company you've placed it.

o: Das Stadion war voll mit Fan.
Das Stadion war voll von Fänse.
de.r: "Voller Fans" — genitive-flavoured, old sport, no preposition required at all here. Shall I repeat it, or are you finally taking notes?

o: สนามกีฬาเต็มไปด้วยแฟนบอล
สนามกีฬาเต็มด้วยไปแฟนบอล
สนามกีฬาไปเต็มด้วยแฟนบอล
สนามกีฬาเต็มไปแฟนบอลด้วย
th.f: สนามกีฬาเต็มไปด้วยแฟนบอล
th.r: เต็มไปด้วย is a fixed little trio — full, go, with — don't try to improve on it, Thai already perfected ‘filled with' centuries before you arrived.

af.r: "Vol ondersteuners" — full of supporters — needs no "van" (of) to bridge adjective and noun; Afrikaans simply rams them together, rather like fans at the gate.

sports.s: I am cheering for Real Madrid.

o: Faccio il tifo per il Real Madrid.
Faccio il tifo al Real Madrid.
Faccio il tifo del Real Madrid.
Faccio il tifo su Real Madrid.
it.f: Faccio il tifo per il Real Madrid.
it.r: "Per il Real Madrid" — "per", old sport, the standard way to cheer for a team in Italian. A modicum of consistency, at least in sport, would be refreshing.

o: Je supporte pour le Real Madrid.
fr.r: "Je supporte le Real Madrid" — the verb takes its object directly in French, old sport, no preposition needed at all. A modicum of consistency, at least in sport.

o: Ich bin Fan von Real Madrid.
Ich bin Fan für Real Madrid.
Ich bin Fan zu Real Madrid.
Ich bin Fan an Real Madrid.
de.f: Ich bin Fan von Real Madrid.
de.r: "Fan von" — the fixed phrase, my dear sir, "von" and nothing else. A modicum of consistency, at least in your loyalties, if not your prepositions.

o: ฉันเชียร์เรอัลมาดริด
ฉันเรอัลมาดริดเชียร์
เชียร์ฉันเรอัลมาดริด
ฉันเชียร์มาดริดเรอัล
th.f: ฉันเชียร์เรอัลมาดริด
th.r: เชียร์ is a borrowed word that behaves like a proper Thai verb — straight onto its object, no ‘for' trailing behind like a confused tourist.

af.r: "Ondersteun" is directly transitive here — no "for" required, unlike English's "cheer for". Real Madrid is supported outright, no preposition standing politely in between.

sports.s: The athlete broke his personal record.

o: L'atleta ha battuto il suo record personale.
L'atleta ha rotto il suo record personale.
L'atleta ha vinto il suo record personale.
L'atleta ha battuto il suo record personale personale.
it.f: L'atleta ha battuto il suo record personale.
it.r: "Ha battuto il record" — the right verb, my dear sir, not "rotto" nor "vinto", both of which describe breaking or winning something else entirely. Unexpected, but correct.

o: L'athlète a battu son record personnel.
L'athlète a cassé son record personnels.
L'athlète a gagné son record personnel.
L'athlète a battu son record personnelle.
fr.f: L'athlète a battu son record personnel.
fr.r: "Battu son record" — the irregular participle of "battre", my dear sir, correctly chosen. Unexpected, but correct — do savour the novelty.

o: Der Athlet hat seinen persönlichen Rekord gebrochen.
Der Athlet hat seinen persönlichen Rekord geschlagen.
Der Athlet hat seinen persönlichen Rekord gewonnen.
Der Athlet hat sein persönlichen Rekord gebrochen.
de.f: Der Athlet hat seinen persönlichen Rekord gebrochen.
de.r: "Seinen persönlichen Rekord" — accusative masculine throughout, old sport, every ending exactly where it belongs. Unexpected, but entirely correct.

o: นักกีฬาทำลายสถิติส่วนตัวของเขา
นักกีฬาทำลายส่วนตัวสถิติของเขา
นักกีฬาสถิติทำลายส่วนตัวของเขา
นักกีฬาทำลายสถิติของส่วนตัวเขา
th.f: นักกีฬาทำลายสถิติส่วนตัวของเขา
th.r: ของเขา trails the noun it owns, Thai-style — possession comes after, like a polite afterthought rather than an English title stamped up front.

o: Die atleet het sy persoonlike rekord gebreek.
Die atleet het sy persoonlike rekord gebroke.
Die atleet het sy persoonlik rekord gebreek.
Die het atleet sy persoonlike rekord gebreek.
af.f: Die atleet het sy persoonlike rekord gebreek.
af.r: "Persoonlike rekord" sits in its expected order, and "gebreek" carries the familiar "ge-" prefix. The athlete, like the grammar, has broken cleanly through.

sports.s: We need a bigger pitch.

o: Abbiamo bisogno di un campo più grande.
Abbiamo bisogno di un campo più grande ancora.
Abbiamo bisogno di un campo più più grande.
Abbiamo bisogno di un campo grande più.
it.f: Abbiamo bisogno di un campo più grande.
it.r: "Più grande", my dear fellow — once is quite enough. "Più più grande" doubles the comparative as though size itself needed repeating.

o: Nous avons besoin d'un terrain plus grand.
Nous avons besoin d'un terrain plus grande.
Nous avons besoin d'un plus grande terrain.
Nous avons besoin d'un terrain plus plus grand.
fr.f: Nous avons besoin d'un terrain plus grand.
fr.r: "Plus grand", my dear fellow — the comparative alone suffices. "Plus plus grand" is a pleonasm that cries out for vengeance, and I shall provide it.

o: Wir brauchen ein mehr größeres Spielfeld.
Wir brauchen ein größeres Spielfeld mehr.
de.r: "Größeres" — the comparative does the work alone, old sport, no "mehr" required alongside it. A pleonasm that cries for vengeance, which you have now received.

o: เราต้องการสนามที่ใหญ่กว่านี้
เราต้องการสนามใหญ่ที่กว่านี้
เราต้องการที่สนามใหญ่กว่านี้
เราสนามต้องการที่ใหญ่กว่านี้
th.f: เราต้องการสนามที่ใหญ่กว่านี้
th.r: ที่ introduces the whole ‘bigger than this' clause tacked onto สนาม — skip it and you're just shouting ‘pitch bigger this', which, admittedly, has its own charm.

o: Ons het 'n meer groot veld nodig.
af.r: The comparative "groter" — bigger — precedes the noun as expected, and "het ... nodig" makes its third appearance in this lesson alone. The pitch, like the soup and the accommodation before it, is formally declared necessary.

sports.s: He injured his knee.

o: Si è infortunato al suoi ginocchio.
it.r: "Al ginocchio" — "a" plus "il" contracts to "al", old sport, exactly as it should. Simple, clean, surgical — rather unlike the knee itself, presumably.

o: Il s'est blessé à sa genou.
Il s'est blessé sur le genou.
fr.r: "Au genou" — "à" plus "le" contracts neatly, old sport, no "sur" wandering in from a different injury entirely. Simple, clean, surgical.

o: Er hat sich am Knie verletzt.
Er hat sich an sein Knie verletzt.
Er hat sich auf dem Knie verletzt.
de.f: Er hat sich am Knie verletzt.
de.r: "Am Knie" — "an" plus "dem" contracts to "am", my dear sir, the standard way to locate an injury. Simple, clean, surgical, unlike your original attempt.

o: เขาบาดเจ็บที่หัวเข่า
เขาบาดเจ็บหัวเข่าที่
เขาบาดที่เจ็บหัวเข่า
บาดเจ็บเขาที่หัวเข่า
th.f: เขาบาดเจ็บที่หัวเข่า
th.r: ที่ pins the injury to the exact knee — leave it out and the injury floats about his entire body, which sounds considerably worse.

af.r: "Beseer" takes its object directly — his knee — no preposition required, unlike English's fondness for "injured ... on" or "at". Straight to the point, rather like the injury itself.

sports.s: The championship finishes next week.

o: Il campionato finisce la prossima settimana.
Il campionato finiscono la prossima settimana.
Il campionato finire la prossima settimana.
Il campionato finisce alla prossima settimana.
it.f: Il campionato finisce la prossima settimana.
it.r: "Finisce" — third person singular, my dear sir, not the plural "finiscono" borrowed from a sentence about several championships. The bench awaits.

o: Le championnat se termine la semaine prochaine.
Le championnat se terminent la semaine prochaine.
Le championnat termine la semaine prochaine.
Le championnat se termine à la semaine prochaine.
fr.f: Le championnat se termine la semaine prochaine.
fr.r: "Se termine", my dear sir — present tense, reflexive, for an event not yet finished. The bench awaits you until your tenses improve.

o: Die Meisterschaft endet in nächster Woche.
Die Meisterschaft wird nächste Woche enden gehabt.
de.r: "Endet" — third person singular, old sport, its "-et" ending firmly in place. The bench awaits you, much like your verb conjugations.

o: การแข่งขันชิงแชมป์จะจบสัปดาห์หน้า
การแข่งขันชิงแชมป์จะจบหน้าสัปดาห์
การแข่งขันจะชิงแชมป์จบสัปดาห์หน้า
การแข่งขันชิงแชมป์จบจะสัปดาห์หน้า
th.f: การแข่งขันชิงแชมป์จะจบสัปดาห์หน้า
th.r: จะ announces the future before the verb, politely warning you it hasn't happened yet — and สัปดาห์หน้า waits at the end, patient as ever.

o: Die kampioenskap eindig in volgende week.
af.r: The present tense "eindig" does the work of a scheduled future here — no "sal" (will) required — and "volgende week" trails to the end. Afrikaans trusts context to carry the future tense's weight.

sports.s: She won a gold medal.

o: Ha vinto una medaglia d'oro d'oro.
Ha vinto una medaglia di oro.
it.r: "Medaglia d'oro" — the fixed phrase, old sport, not "d'ora", which means something else entirely and considerably less golden. You may take a lap of honour.

o: Elle a gagné une médaille d'or.
Elle a gagné une médaille en ors.
Elle a gagné une médaille dorée.
Elle a gagné une médaille de l'or.
fr.f: Elle a gagné une médaille d'or.
fr.r: "Médaille d'or" — the fixed compound, old sport, "en ors" and "de l'or" both imposters here. You may take a lap of honour, grammar notwithstanding.

o: Sie hat eine goldenes Medaille gewonnen.
Sie hat eine Medaille von Gold gewonnen.
Sie hat eine Medaille Gold gewonnen.
de.r: "Goldmedaille" — one glorious German compound, my dear sir, not scattered across several words. You may take a lap of honour; the compound noun certainly deserves one.

o: เธอได้เหรียญทอง
เธอได้ทองเหรียญ
เธอเหรียญทองได้
ได้เธอเหรียญทอง
th.f: เธอได้เหรียญทอง
th.r: ได้เหรียญทอง needs no article fussing about ‘a' medal — Thai doesn't count your golds, it simply hands them to you, got.

af.r: "Goue" is the adjective form of "goud" (gold), taking that telltale "-e" ending before the noun. Gold becomes golden, rather as a biltong strip becomes a proper feast.

sports.s: The coach gave us good information.

o: L'allenatore ci ha dato buone informazioni.
L'allenatore ci ha dato delle buoni informazioni.
L'allenatore ci ha dato di buoni informazioni.
L'allenatore ci ha dato una buona informazioni.
it.f: L'allenatore ci ha dato buone informazioni.
it.r: "Buone informazioni" — plural agreement throughout, my dear sir, not "delle buoni" mixing singular and plural like a confused buffet. Try again, you may be luckier.

o: L'entraîneur nous a donné de bonnes informations.
L'entraîneur nous a donné des bonnes informations.
L'entraîneur nous a donné de bons informations.
L'entraîneur nous a donné des bonne information.
fr.f: L'entraîneur nous a donné de bonnes informations.
fr.r: "De bonnes informations" — the plural adjective takes "de" before it, my dear sir, as French so often insists. Try again; you may be luckier.

o: Der Trainer hat uns gute Informationen gegeben.
Der Trainer hat uns guter Information gegeben.
Der Trainer hat uns guten Informationen gegeben.
Der Trainer hat uns gute Informazionen gegeben.
de.f: Der Trainer hat uns gute Informationen gegeben.
de.r: "Gute Informationen" — plural, uninflected beyond its ending, old sport, no invented "Informazionen" borrowed from a language you don't speak. Try again.

o: โค้ชให้ข้อมูลดี ๆ กับเรา
โค้ชให้ดี ๆ ข้อมูลกับเรา
โค้ชให้ข้อมูลกับดี ๆ เรา
โค้ชข้อมูลดี ๆ ให้เรากับ
th.f: โค้ชให้ข้อมูลดี ๆ กับเรา
th.r: ดี ๆ repeats itself for a touch of emphasis — one ‘ดี' is merely good, doubled it's properly good, rather like ordering spice level twice at a som tam stall.

o: Die afrigter het vir ons goeie inligting gegee.
Die afrigter het vir ons goeie inligtings gegee.
Die afrigter het gegee vir ons goeie inligting.
Die het afrigter vir ons goeie inligting gegee.
af.f: Die afrigter het vir ons goeie inligting gegee.
af.r: "Vir ons" marks the recipients, and "goeie" is "goed" dressed up with its "-e" ending before a noun — the adjectival form, standing smartly to attention.

sports.s: I watched the match on television.

o: Ho guardato la partita in televisione.
Ho guardato la partita a televisione.
Ho guardato la partita sulla televisione.
Ho guardato la partita nella televisione.
it.f: Ho guardato la partita in televisione.
it.r: "In televisione", my dear sir — no article needed, unlike "sulla" or "nella", both of which overcomplicate a perfectly simple broadcast. At least you haven't failed on media.

o: J'ai regardé le match à la télévision.
J'ai regardé le match à la télés.
J'ai regardé le match sur la télévision.
J'ai regardé le match dans la télévision.
fr.f: J'ai regardé le match à la télévision.
fr.r: "À la télévision", my dear sir — the fixed phrase for watching something broadcast. At least you haven't failed on the subject of media itself.

o: Ich habe das Spiel im Fernsehen gesehen.
Ich habe das Spiel am Fernsehen gesehen.
Ich habe das Spiel auf Fernsehen gesehen.
Ich habe das Spiel in der Fernsehen gesehen.
de.f: Ich habe das Spiel im Fernsehen gesehen.
de.r: "Im Fernsehen" — "in" plus "dem" contracts to "im", old sport, the standard home of anything watched on screen. At least you haven't failed on media.

o: ฉันดูการแข่งขันทางโทรทัศน์
ฉันดูทางโทรทัศน์การแข่งขัน
ฉันทางดูการแข่งขันโทรทัศน์
ฉันการแข่งขันดูทางโทรทัศน์
th.f: ฉันดูการแข่งขันทางโทรทัศน์
th.r: ทาง marks ‘via television' — drop it and you're watching the match travel through the TV itself, which is a more literal experience than intended.

o: Ek het die wedstryd op televisie gekyk.
Ek het die wedstryd op televisie gekijk.
Ek het gekyk die wedstryd op televisie.
Ek die het wedstryd op televisie gekyk.
af.f: Ek het die wedstryd op televisie gekyk.
af.r: "Op televisie" — on television — uses "op", not "in", for the medium. The match was watched upon the screen, as it were, rather than inside it.

sports.s: They played with only ten players.

o: Hanno giocato con soli dieci giocatori.
Hanno giocato con soli dieci giocatore.
Hanno giocato con dieci giocatori solo.
Hanno giocato per soli dieci giocatori.
it.f: Hanno giocato con soli dieci giocatori.
it.r: "Con soli dieci giocatori" — "soli" agrees with the players, old sport, not trailing alone at the sentence's end like an eleventh man sent off. Let's call it a draw.

o: Ils ont joué avec seulement dix joueurs.
Ils ont joué avec dix joueur seulement.
Ils ont joué avec que dix joueurs.
Ils ont joué par dix joueurs seulement.
fr.f: Ils ont joué avec seulement dix joueurs.
fr.r: "Avec seulement dix joueurs" — "seulement" precedes the number it limits, old sport, not trailing uselessly behind it. Let's call it a draw, grammatically speaking.

o: Sie haben mit nur zehn Spielern gespielt.
Sie haben mit zehn Spielern nur gespielt.
Sie haben mit nur zehn Spieler gespielt.
Sie haben bei nur zehn Spielern gespielt.
de.f: Sie haben mit nur zehn Spielern gespielt.
de.r: "Mit nur zehn Spielern" — dative plural, my dear sir, "Spielern" with its "-n" intact. Let's call it a draw, though your case endings lost outright.

o: พวกเขาเล่นกันแค่สิบคน
พวกเขาเล่นกันสิบแค่คน
พวกเขากันเล่นแค่สิบคน
พวกเขาเล่นแค่กันคนสิบ
th.f: พวกเขาเล่นกันแค่สิบคน
th.r: กัน signals they did it together, and แค่สิบคน keeps the classifier คน right after the number — ten people, properly counted, not ten of something stranger.

o: Hulle het met net tien spelers gespeel.
Hulle het met net tien spelers gespeelt.
Hulle het net met tien speler gespeel.
Hulle met het net tien spelers gespeel.
af.f: Hulle het met net tien spelers gespeel.
af.r: "Met net tien spelers" places "net" (only) directly before the number, tucked snugly against it. Ten players, no more, no fewer, and no ambiguity about where "only" belongs.

culture.s: That museum was amazing.

it.r: "Era" — imperfect, singular, my dear sir, the tense for a lingering impression. "Ha stato" is an auxiliary error so bold it's almost impressive.

fr.r: "Était" — imperfect, singular, my dear sir, not a plural wandering in from a different museum entirely. Contemporary art makes more sense than your agreement does.

de.r: "War" — singular past tense, old sport, matching a singular museum. "Waren" would suggest you visited several at once, which, grammatically, you did not.

o: พิพิธภัณฑ์นั้นยอดเยี่ยมมาก
พิพิธภัณฑ์ยอดเยี่ยมนั้นมาก
นั้นพิพิธภัณฑ์ยอดเยี่ยมมาก
พิพิธภัณฑ์นั้นมากยอดเยี่ยม
th.f: พิพิธภัณฑ์นั้นยอดเยี่ยมมาก
th.r: นั้น trails the noun it's pointing at — Thai demonstratives follow, they don't lead, unlike an English tour guide marching ahead shouting ‘that museum!'

af.r: "Daardie" — that — contrasts with "hierdie" (this), and "asemrowend" fuses "asem" (breath) with "rowend" (robbing) into one splendidly vivid compound: breath-robbing. English's "amazing" feels rather pale by comparison.

culture.s: Who did you see at the gallery?

o: Chi tu hai visto alla galleria?
Chi è che hai vedere alla galleria?
it.r: "Chi hai visto?" — the participle, correctly chosen, my dear sir, not the bare infinitive "vedere" standing in confusedly for it. So simple, yet so far beyond you.

o: Tu as vu qui à la galerie ?
Qui as-tu vu à la galerie ?
Qui tu as vu à la galerie ?
Qui as-tu voir à la galerie ?
fr.f: Tu as vu qui à la galerie ?
fr.natural_version: Tu as vu qui à la galerie ?
fr.literal_trap: Qui as-tu vu à la galerie ?
fr.native_context: ‘Qui as-tu vu’ is written French; speech keeps the normal word order: ‘Tu as vu qui ?’
fr.roast_if_wrong: ‘Qui as-tu vu’, how literary. In the café, people say ‘Tu as vu qui ?’
fr.r: "Qui tu as vu" skips the inversion entirely, standing about without its question mark's proper manners, and "voir" in the final option is a bare infinitive where a past participle, "vu", was required.

o: Wen hast du in der Galerie gesehen?
Wen du hast in der Galerie gesehen?
Wen hast du in der Galerie sehen?
Wen hast du in der Galerie gesehen gehabt?
de.f: Wen hast du in der Galerie gesehen?
de.r: "Wen hast du gesehen?" — accusative "wen" for the object seen, old sport, never nominative "wer". So simple a question, yet so thoroughly undone.

o: คุณเจอใครที่แกลเลอรี
คุณใครเจอที่แกลเลอรี
คุณเจอที่แกลเลอรีใคร
เจอคุณใครที่แกลเลอรี
th.f: คุณเจอใครที่แกลเลอรี
th.r: ใคร stays right where the answer would go, after เจอ — Thai doesn't drag its question words to the front like a suspect for interrogation.

o: Wie het jy by die galery gesien?
Wie jy het by die galery gesien?
Wie is jy by die galery gesien?
Wie het jy by die gesien galery?
af.f: Wie het jy by die galery gesien?
af.r: "Wie" triggers the familiar inversion — verb leaping ahead to meet its question word — and "by die galery" is, once again, "at" rather than "in". The gallery, like the hotel earlier, is visited "by".

culture.s: The painting is unique.

o: Il dipinto è il più unico.
it.r: "Unico" admits no comparative, my dear sir, however tempting "più unico" sounds. One cannot be more unique, only more mistaken.

o: Le tableau est le plus unique.
fr.r: "Unique" admits no comparative, my dear sir — one cannot be "more unique" any more than one can be "more pregnant". Absolute adjectives, absolutely non-negotiable.

de.r: "Einzigartig" — an absolute adjective, old sport, immune to comparison in German exactly as in French. One cannot be "more unique"; one simply is.

o: ภาพวาดนี้ไม่เหมือนใคร
ภาพวาดนี้เหมือนไม่ใคร
ภาพวาดไม่นี้เหมือนใคร
นี้ภาพวาดไม่เหมือนใคร
th.f: ภาพวาดนี้ไม่เหมือนใคร
th.r: ไม่เหมือนใคร literally means ‘resembles no one' — a properly poetic way to call something unique, and a fixed phrase you don't get to rearrange.

af.r: Plain and correct, old chap — though do note "skildery" (painting) shares its root with "skilder" (to paint, or painter), a tidy little family of words worth knowing.

culture.s: She read a book about Italian history.

o: Ha letto un libro sulla storia italiana.
Ha letto un libro sulla storia italiano.
Ha letto un libro sulla storia d'Italiano.
Ha letto un libro su storia italiana.
it.f: Ha letto un libro sulla storia italiana.
it.r: "Storia italiana" — feminine agreement throughout, old sport, "italiano" alone leaves the sentence limping. The basics of civilisation, I'm afraid, still elude you.

o: Elle a lu un livre sur l'histoire italienne.
Elle a lu un livre sur l'histoire italien.
Elle a lu un livre sur l'histoire de italie.
Elle a lu un livre sur histoire italienne.
fr.f: Elle a lu un livre sur l'histoire italienne.
fr.r: "L'histoire italienne" — adjective agreeing in gender, old sport, "italien" without its silent feminine "-ne" simply refuses to match "histoire". The basics of civilisation, really.

o: Sie hat ein Buch über die italienische Geschichte gelesen.
Sie hat ein Buch über die italienisch Geschichte gelesen.
Sie hat ein Buch über Geschichte italienisch gelesen.
Sie hat ein Buch über die Geschichte Italien gelesen.
de.f: Sie hat ein Buch über die italienische Geschichte gelesen.
de.r: "Italienische Geschichte" — the adjective takes its ending before a feminine noun, my dear sir, not left bare as though German had no genders at all. The basics of civilisation.

o: เธออ่านหนังสือเกี่ยวกับประวัติศาสตร์อิตาลี
เธออ่านหนังสือเกี่ยวกับอิตาลีประวัติศาสตร์
เธอหนังสืออ่านเกี่ยวกับประวัติศาสตร์อิตาลี
เธออ่านประวัติศาสตร์เกี่ยวกับหนังสืออิตาลี
th.f: เธออ่านหนังสือเกี่ยวกับประวัติศาสตร์อิตาลี
th.r: เกี่ยวกับ introduces what the book concerns — without it, she's just reading a book that happens to be in the same room as Italian history.

o: Sy het 'n boek oor Italiaanse geskiedenis gelees.
Sy het 'n boek oor Italiaans geskiedenis gelees.
Sy is 'n boek oor Italiaanse geskiedenis gelees.
Sy 'n het boek oor Italiaanse geskiedenis gelees.
af.f: Sy het 'n boek oor Italiaanse geskiedenis gelees.
af.r: "Oor" marks the topic — about — and "Italiaanse" is the adjectival form of "Italiaans", properly inflected before the noun it describes.

culture.s: He is interested in art.

it.r: "All'arte" — the contracted preposition, my dear sir, "a" plus "l'arte" fusing neatly. "Per l'arte" or "con l'arte" are impostors in borrowed clothing.

fr.r: "S'intéresse à", my dear sir — the reflexive verb with "à", never "pour" nor "de", both imposters borrowed from entirely different constructions.

de.r: "Sich interessieren für" — "für", old sport, the fixed preposition, never "an" nor "mit". Interesting, how consistently you err in exactly the wrong direction.

o: เขาสนใจศิลปะ
เขาศิลปะสนใจ
สนใจเขาศิลปะ
เขาสนศิลปะใจ
th.f: เขาสนใจศิลปะ
th.r: สนใจ already means ‘interested in' as one word — tack on an extra preposition and you've politely interested him twice.

af.r: "Belangstel in" — be interested in — is a separable compound verb, splitting as "stel belang in". The interest gets planted ("stel") directly into the thing itself, a rather charmingly literal image.

culture.s: The concert was very successful.

o: Il concerto è stato un grande successo.
Il concerto è stato un grande successi.
Il concerto è stato un grande successo grande.
Il concerto è stato molto successo.
it.f: Il concerto è stato un grande successo.
it.r: "Un grande successo" — singular, unadorned, old sport, not doubled into "successo grande" as though one triumph required saying twice. Redo both the grammar and the modesty.

o: Le concert a été un grand succès.
Le concert a été un grand succés.
Le concert était un grand succès.
Le concert a été très succès.
fr.f: Le concert a été un grand succès.
fr.r: "Un grand succès" — correctly spelled, old sport, unlike "succés" with its wandering accent aigu masquerading as something it isn't. Spelling and grammar both to be redone.

o: Das Konzert war ein großer Erfolg.
Das Konzert war ein großen Erfolg.
Das Konzert hat ein großer Erfolg gewesen.
de.f: Das Konzert war ein großer Erfolg.
de.r: "Ein großer Erfolg" — masculine nominative ending, my dear sir, "großen" belongs to an entirely different case. Spelling and grammar both to be redone, I'm afraid.

o: คอนเสิร์ตประสบความสำเร็จอย่างมาก
คอนเสิร์ตประสบสำเร็จความอย่างมาก
คอนเสิร์ตประสบอย่างมากความสำเร็จ
ประสบคอนเสิร์ตความสำเร็จอย่างมาก
th.f: คอนเสิร์ตประสบความสำเร็จอย่างมาก
th.r: ประสบความสำเร็จ is a fixed trio meaning ‘to succeed' — pull it apart and the concert merely experiences something vague, which is far less impressive.

af.r: Plain and correct — a great success stands just as proudly in Afrikaans as in English, with no hidden traps lurking in the grammar this time.

culture.s: We went to see an exhibition.

o: Siamo andati a vedere una mostra.
Siamo andati per vedere una mostra.
Abbiamo andato a vedere una mostra.
Siamo andati a vedere una esposizione.
it.f: Siamo andati a vedere una mostra.
it.r: "A vedere", my dear sir — "a" before the infinitive of purpose, never "per vedere" substituted in without the sentence's permission. Stop inventing surreal structures.

o: Nous sommes allés voir une exposition.
Nous sommes allés pour à voir une exposition.
Nous avons allé voir une exposition.
Nous sommes allés à voir une exposition.
fr.f: Nous sommes allés voir une exposition.
fr.r: "Allés voir" — the infinitive follows directly, my dear sir, no stray preposition inserted between "aller" and its purpose. Do stop inventing surreal structures.

o: Wir sind zu einer Ausstellung gegangen.
Wir sind zu einer Ausstellung gehen.
Wir haben zu einer Ausstellung gegangen.
Wir sind für eine Ausstellung gegangen.
de.f: Wir sind zu einer Ausstellung gegangen.
de.r: "Sind gegangen" — perfect tense with "sein", old sport, as a trip to an exhibition is, after all, motion. Do stop inventing surreal structures of your own.

o: เราไปชมนิทรรศการ
เราชมไปนิทรรศการ
ไปเราชมนิทรรศการ
เราไปนิทรรศการชม
th.f: เราไปชมนิทรรศการ
th.r: ไปชม strings ‘go' and ‘view' back to back — Thai doesn't need ‘to see' tacked on with a preposition, it just goes and looks.

af.r: "Gaan kyk" — went to look — pairs two verbs directly, with no "om...te" infinitive bridge needed. Afrikaans allows this neat double-verb shortcut for movement with purpose.

culture.s: The actor played his role perfectly.

o: L'attore ha recitato il suo ruolo perfettamente.
L'attore ha recitato il suo ruolo perfetto.
L'attore ha recitato il suo ruolo perfezione.
L'attore ha recitato perfettamente il suo ruolo perfetto.
it.f: L'attore ha recitato il suo ruolo perfettamente.
it.r: "Perfettamente" — the adverb, my dear sir, not "perfetto" twice over as though the role itself needed double perfection. Your performance here is imperfect.

o: L'acteur a joué son rôle parfaitement.
L'acteur a joué son rôle parfait.
L'acteur a joué son rôle perfection.
L'acteur a joué parfaitement son rôle parfait.
fr.f: L'acteur a joué son rôle parfaitement.
fr.r: "Parfaitement" — the adverb, my dear sir, not "parfait" doubled as though perfection needed repeating. Your performance here, alas, remains rather imperfect.

o: Der Schauspieler hat seine Rolle perfekt gespielt.
Der Schauspieler hat seine Rolle perfekte gespielt.
Der Schauspieler hat seine Rolle Perfektion gespielt.
Der Schauspieler hat seine Rolle perfekt gespielt gehabt.
de.f: Der Schauspieler hat seine Rolle perfekt gespielt.
de.r: "Perfekt" — uninflected as an adverb, old sport, "perfekte" belongs only before a noun. Your performance here is imperfect, unlike the actor's.

o: นักแสดงเล่นบทบาทของเขาได้อย่างสมบูรณ์แบบ
นักแสดงเล่นบทบาทของเขาอย่างได้สมบูรณ์แบบ
นักแสดงบทบาทเล่นของเขาได้อย่างสมบูรณ์แบบ
นักแสดงเล่นของบทบาทเขาได้อย่างสมบูรณ์แบบ
th.f: นักแสดงเล่นบทบาทของเขาได้อย่างสมบูรณ์แบบ
th.r: ได้อย่าง bridges the verb to its adverb of manner — skip it and you've simply stated he ‘played perfect', which is a compliment to his acting, not his grammar.

o: Die akteur het sy rol perfek gespeel.
Die akteur het sy rol perfekt gespeel.
Die akteur het perfek sy rol gespeel.
Die het akteur sy rol perfek gespeel.
af.f: Die akteur het sy rol perfek gespeel.
af.r: "Perfek gespeel" places the adverb before the past participle, not trailing after as English prefers. The role was "perfectly played", word order and performance both impeccable.

culture.s: This is a book written by Dante.

o: Questo è un libro scritto da Dante.
Questo è un libro scrivuto da Dante.
Questo è un libro scrivendo da Dante.
Questo è un libro che scritto da Dante.
it.f: Questo è un libro scritto da Dante.
it.r: "Scritto" — the irregular past participle of "scrivere", my dear sir, not "scrivuto", a word that exists nowhere but in your imagination. Dante would turn in his grave.

o: C'est un livre écrit par Dante.
C'est un livre écrit de Dante.
C'est un livre écrivé par Dante.
C'est un livre qui est écrire par Dante.
fr.f: C'est un livre écrit par Dante.
fr.r: "Écrit par", my dear sir — the correct past participle, never "écrivé", an invention Dante would find personally insulting.

o: Das ist ein Buch, das von Dante geschrieben wurde.
Das ist ein Buch geschrieben von Dante.
Das ist ein Buch schrieb von Dante.
Das ist ein Buch von Dante geschreibt.
de.f: Das ist ein Buch, das von Dante geschrieben wurde.
de.r: "Geschriebenes" — the participle used adjectivally, old sport, declined to agree with "Buch". Dante would turn in his grave, and rightly so.

o: นี่คือหนังสือที่ดันเต้เขียน
นี่คือหนังสือเขียนที่ดันเต้
นี่หนังสือคือที่ดันเต้เขียน
นี่คือที่หนังสือดันเต้เขียน
th.f: นี่คือหนังสือที่ดันเต้เขียน
th.r: ที่ introduces exactly what Dante did to the book — drop it and you've simply announced ‘this is book Dante wrote', like a caveman reviewing the Divine Comedy.

o: Dit is 'n boek wat deur Dante geskryf is.
Dit is 'n boek wat deur Dante geskrijf is.
Dit is 'n boek wat Dante deur geskryf is.
Dit 'n is boek wat deur Dante geskryf is.
af.f: Dit is 'n boek wat deur Dante geskryf is.
af.r: The passive voice assembles itself as "wat deur ... geskryf is" — which by ... written is — with the relative "wat", the passive marker "deur" (by), and "is" bringing up the rear. A proper procession of grammar, rather like a parade.

culture.s: She has a great knowledge of art.

o: Ha una grande cultura in arte.
Ha una grande conoscenza in arte.
it.r: "Conoscenza dell'arte" — "di" plus "l'arte" contracts to "dell'", my dear sir, exactly as French does with "de l'art". False friends always catch you out.

o: Elle a une grande connaissance de l'art.
Elle a une grande culture en art.
Elle a une grande connaissance dans art.
Elle a une grande connaissance à l'art.
fr.f: Elle a une grande connaissance de l'art.
fr.r: "Une grande connaissance de l'art" — "connaissance", my dear sir, not "savoir", a false friend English speakers fall for with depressing regularity.

o: Sie kennt sich mit Kunst sehr gut aus.
Sie kennt sich mit Kunst sehr gut an.
Sie kennt sich mit Kunst aus sehr gut.
Sie kennt mit Kunst sehr gut sich aus.
de.f: Sie kennt sich mit Kunst sehr gut aus.
de.r: "Sich auskennen mit" is the fixed phrase for being knowledgeable about something — swap "aus" for "an", and the meaning rather falls apart. And that separable prefix "aus" belongs at the very end of the clause, not loitering in the middle, nor should "sich" go wandering off to the back of the queue.

o: เธอมีความรู้ด้านศิลปะมาก
เธอมีความรู้ศิลปะด้านมาก
เธอมีด้านความรู้ศิลปะมาก
เธอความรู้มีด้านศิลปะมาก
th.f: เธอมีความรู้ด้านศิลปะมาก
th.r: ด้าน marks exactly which field her knowledge covers — without it, she simply has a great deal of knowledge, direction unspecified, which is a bold but vague claim.

o: Sy het groot kennis van kuns.
Sy het groot kennis aan kuns.
Sy het kennis groot van kuns.
Sy groot het kennis van kuns.
af.f: Sy het groot kennis van kuns.
af.r: "Kennis van" — knowledge of — is the fixed preposition pairing, and "groot" here means "great" in the abstract sense, not merely "large" in girth.

culture.s: The theatre was empty.

o: Il teatro era vuoto da gente.
Il teatro era vuoto in gente.
Il teatro era vuoto con gente.
it.r: "Vuoto" — masculine agreement with "teatro", my dear sir, unadorned and correct. Fewer words, fewer errors — a lesson the theatre apparently taught you.

o: Le théâtre était vide des gens.
Le théâtre était vide en gens.
Le théâtre était vide avec gens.
fr.r: "Vide", my dear sir — one adjective, no article needed. Fewer words, fewer opportunities for error; the theatre, like your sentence, was refreshingly empty.

o: Das Theater war leer von Mensch.
Das Theater war leer an Menschen.
Das Theater war leer mit Menschen.
de.r: "Leer" — uninflected after "war", old sport, as predicate adjectives in German so sensibly remain. Fewer words, fewer errors, more empty theatres.

o: โรงละครว่างเปล่า
โรงละครเปล่าว่าง
ละครโรงว่างเปล่า
โรงว่างละครเปล่า
th.f: โรงละครว่างเปล่า
th.r: ว่างเปล่า doubles down on empty for emphasis — Thai doesn't do ‘very empty', it simply says the word twice and lets you feel the silence.

af.r: Plain and correct — though you might note "teater" keeps its tidy Afrikaans spelling, no "th" cluster needed, unlike its English cousin.

culture.s: We listened to classical music.

it.r: "Ascoltato musica classica" — the participle agrees with nothing feminine required here, old sport, "ascoltata" would be simply wrong. Listen to me, for once.

o: Nous avons écouté de la musique classique.
Nous avons écouté le musique classique.
Nous avons écouté à la musique classique.
Nous avons écouté de musique classique.
fr.f: Nous avons écouté de la musique classique.
fr.r: "De la musique classique" — the partitive article, old sport, before an uncountable noun. Listen to me, for once, the way you failed to listen to the orchestra.

o: Wir haben zu klassischer Musik gehört.
Wir haben auf klassische Musik gehört.
de.r: "Klassische Musik" — accusative, uninflected beyond its adjective ending, my dear sir, no article needed at all. Listen to me, for once, if not to Mozart.

o: เราฟังดนตรีคลาสสิก
เราฟังคลาสสิกดนตรี
เราดนตรีฟังคลาสสิก
ฟังเราดนตรีคลาสสิก
th.f: เราฟังดนตรีคลาสสิก
th.r: ฟัง already means ‘listen to' — add a stray ‘to' in your head and Thai will wonder what exactly you're listening toward.

o: Ons het na klassieke musiek geluister.
Ons het na klassiek musiek geluister.
Ons na het klassieke musiek geluister.
af.f: Ons het na klassieke musiek geluister.
af.r: "Luister na" — listen to — insists on "na", not "aan", which would mean something rather different entirely. Prepositions in Afrikaans, like seasoning in a good bobotie, must be exactly right.

culture.s: The author published a new novel.

o: L'autore ha pubblicato un nuovo romanzo.
L'autore ha pubblicato un nuovo romanzio.
L'autore ha pubblicare un nuovo romanzo.
L'autore ha edito un nuovo romanzo.
it.f: L'autore ha pubblicato un nuovo romanzo.
